newsitem.title: USA: Gehrig uniform sale a sign baseball market is strong.
newsitem.headline: Gehrig uniform sale a sign baseball market is strong.

text.p: The uniform an ailing Lou Gehrig wore when he made his "Luckiest Man Alive" speech on July 4, 1939, sold for $306,000 last month, the highest price ever for a baseball uniform, in a clear sign that baseball memorabilia is back.

The national pastime took a drubbing after the 1994-95 strike, the longest in professional sports. Fans lost interest, attendance tumbled and prices for collectibles, which had been falling for a few years, kept heading south.
But with interest in baseball rising, the market for baseball memorabilia is showing signs of life.

In addition to the uniform that the New York Yankee first baseman wore during his famous speech, all of the 767 other lots offered sold at the auction run by Robert Edward Auctions, the nation's leading baseball collectibles house.
The June 28-29 auction raised about $3.3 million, the highest ever for the auction house.

"This says the industry is extremely strong, much stronger than most of us realised, if you have real memorabilia," said Steven Rotman, a veteran collector who is starting the National Sports Gallery, a museum in Washington.
"It's a very healthy market," said Robert Edward Auctions President Robert Lifson. "What surprised me was the number of people who were enthusiastic bidders on things that were very expensive."

Other items sold at the auction included a Honus Wagner card from 1909 for about $119,000, a Mickey Mantle uniform for $85,000 and the ball President John Kennedy threw out to open the 1962 season and later autographed that fetched about $30,800. All prices include a 15 percent commission.

Experts said fans and collectors have finally forgiven the players and owners for the 232-day strike. "If this same auction had occurred during the strike, it would have been half the amount," said Rotman, of Worcestor, Mass.

While many items at the auction did not set records, the prices were generally strong, reflecting solid demand for quality, vintage items with a well documented history, the collectors and historians said.

For example, the Honus Wagner card sold last month fetched only a fraction of the $640,500 that a similar card brought at a Christie's auction in September. But that mint-condition card is the best baseball card in the world, collectors said. The card sold last month, while in very good condition, was "not even in the same room," Lifson said.
The auction underlined the split between true vintage items and newer memorabilia, including cards from the 1980s.
"The market for older vintage material remains real good. If there's been any fall-off in the hobby, it's been mainly in new stuff," said Kit Young, a dealer in San Diego.

Nineteen-eighties cards, which tumbled in price after a big run-up, have recovered some ground but remain well off their peaks, the experts said. Several cautioned against buying them, however, since millions of cards were printed.
"Stay away from the new stuff, it's not going to be worth the cardboard it's printed on," said Ken Felden, who's been collecting baseball items for 20 years.

Overall, the sale offered a strong menu of items presented with painstaking detail to show that they were authentic, baseball lovers said. "It was the most outstanding auction I've ever seen," said Felden.

"I basically spent a solid week studying the catalogue," said Rotman, whose museum, sponsored by MCI Communications Corp., is scheduled to open in December. The sale was an important sign that baseball is returning to health, he said.
"But players have to understand that they represent something more than the dollar bill and have to give something back to the public," he said.

More affordable vintage items include Old Judge cards from the late 19th century that can be worth $2,000 or more in very good condition with Hall of Fame players, collectors said. A few of the cards sold at the auction for under $1,000.
